q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE method Gandhi used to challenge British rule in India.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why Gandhi's methods were effective against the British, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which Indian independence differed from the decolonization of French Algeria.

sample_answers.a: Gandhi organized mass nonviolent campaigns — including the Salt March (1930), boycotts of British goods, and noncooperation with colonial institutions — mobilizing millions of ordinary Indians in peaceful defiance.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, nonviolent resistance put the British in an impossible position: violent repression of peaceful protesters (as at Amritsar in 1919) outraged world opinion and delegitimized British claims to be a civilizing force, while concessions only encouraged further demands.
sample_answers.c: India achieved independence primarily through negotiation and mass political pressure, with the British withdrawing in 1947; Algeria required an eight-year war (1954–62) because French settlers and the French state refused to contemplate Algerian independence, making violent revolution the only path.

q1.stimulus:
Historians describe India's independence movement as distinctive for its scale and its methods. Under Gandhi's leadership, the Indian National Congress transformed from an elite debating society into a mass movement that mobilized peasants, workers, and women across the subcontinent. Gandhi's strategy of satyagraha — nonviolent resistance — was designed to make British rule morally and practically untenable: by courting arrest, boycotting British goods, and refusing cooperation, Indians forced the British to choose between violent repression (which destroyed their legitimacy) and concessions (which emboldened further demands). Yet historians also emphasize the movement's tragic outcome: independence came with the partition of British India into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan, accompanied by horrific communal violence that killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.
—Historian's account of Indian independence in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE criticism Gandhi makes of modern Western civilization.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Gandhi's vision of swaraj (self-rule) differed from simply replacing British officials with Indian ones.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Gandhi's ideas appealed to ordinary Indians beyond the educated elite.

sample_answers.a: Gandhi argues that Western civilization is materialistic and dehumanizing — it measures progress by machinery and wealth while destroying moral and spiritual life, and India should not imitate it.
sample_answers.b: For Gandhi, true self-rule meant not just Indian faces in colonial offices but a transformation of society: village self-sufficiency, rejection of industrial materialism, and moral self-discipline, not merely a change of rulers.
sample_answers.c: Gandhi framed independence in religious and moral language ordinary people understood, wore simple homespun cloth, and focused on concrete grievances like the salt tax — making the movement accessible to peasants, not just lawyers and intellectuals.

q2.stimulus:
It is my deliberate opinion that India is being ground down not under the English heel but under that of modern civilization. It is groaning under the monster's terrible weight. There is no end to the victims it has claimed. This civilization is such that one has only to be patient and it will be self-destroyed. ... My patriotism does not teach me that I am to allow people to be crushed under the heel of Indian princes if only the English retire. If I have the power, I should resist the tyranny of Indian princes just as much as that of the English.
—Adapted from Mohandas Gandhi, Hind Swaraj (Indian Home Rule), 1909

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the photograph that reflects Gandhi's political message.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which Gandhi's personal image served the independence movement.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Gandhi's assassination in 1948 intensified the tragedy of partition.

sample_answers.a: Gandhi wears simple homespun cloth (khadi) rather than Western dress, visually rejecting British manufactured goods and identifying himself with India's poor peasants — a deliberate political statement in every public appearance.
sample_answers.b: His image as a humble, saintly figure in peasant dress made him recognizable worldwide and gave the movement a moral authority that transcended politics; the British found it far harder to discredit a 'holy man' than a conventional politician.
sample_answers.c: Gandhi was the most prominent advocate of Hindu-Muslim unity; his murder by a Hindu extremist symbolized the triumph of the communal hatred he had fought, deepening the sense that partition's violence had destroyed the inclusive India he envisioned.

q3.stimulus: The image is a 1931 studio portrait of Mohandas K. Gandhi, taken in London while he attended the Round Table Conference on India's constitutional future. Gandhi, who led the Indian independence movement through nonviolent resistance, is shown in his characteristic simple dress. By 1931 he was the most recognizable anti-colonial leader in the world, and his image — the loincloth, the spinning wheel, the frail frame — had become a global symbol of resistance to empire.
